sections.content: Lo que + verb, placed at the front of a sentence, works like an English cleft ("what made it radical was...") -- it isolates one element for emphasis, ideal for a reading that wants to spotlight exactly which two articles made the 1917 constitution so unusual. These sentences are taken directly from the previous reading.

items.spanish: Lo que se redactó en la ciudad de Querétaro, en 1917, superó ampliamente cualquier expectativa moderada.
items.english: What was drafted in the city of Querétaro, in 1917, far exceeded any moderate expectation.

items.spanish: Lo que hizo verdaderamente radical a esta nueva constitución fueron dos artículos en particular.
items.english: What made this new constitution truly radical were two articles in particular.

items.spanish: Lo que distinguió a esta constitución de la mayoría de las constituciones liberales del siglo diecinueve fue su ambición social explícita.
items.english: What distinguished this constitution from most nineteenth-century liberal constitutions was its explicit social ambition.

items.spanish: Lo que hace de la Constitución de 1917 un documento tan estudiado, incluso un siglo después, es precisamente esa combinación.
items.english: What makes the 1917 Constitution such a studied document, even a century later, is precisely that combination.

sections.content: The verb after ser can be singular or plural depending on what follows it: lo que... fueron dos artículos (plural, because "two articles" is plural) but lo que... fue su ambición social (singular, matching "ambition") -- ser agrees with the noun on the far side of the sentence, not with lo que itself.
